newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH REGULATOR SAYS BANKS MUST CUT COSTS MORE.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH REGULATOR SAYS BANKS MUST CUT COSTS MORE.

text.p: Finnish banks must continue to cut costs and find ways to boost their revenue, said Kaarlo Jannari, director of the Finnish Financial Supervision (Rata).

In a written copy of a speech to the new cooperative banking group around OKOBANK on Tuesday, he also said Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU) would speed up the ongoing restructuring amid tightening competition for clients.
"Although the acute banking crisis is over for now, Finnish banks' performance is at best satisfactory, and the cooperative banks are no exception," Jannari said.

Jannari said banks' income from financial operations showed no sign of improvement and balance sheets were still burdened by low-yield real estate holdings, and the recovery was due to falling credit losses and gains from selling securities.

In addition, banks still had significant portions of state capital certificates in their capital base "the repayment of which and replacement with private first tier equity can succeed only if banks' results improve significantly".

Jannari said he understood banks' wishes to expand their operations into new areas but added that the law limited the chances to do so, but he also said he would not want to give retailers the right to offer banking services.
"This view is becoming old-fashioned. But if it is so, then banks should be able to sell sausages, not to mention insurances and postal services," he said.
"From the point of view of the financial sector, EMU is in fact just part of the fast (global) internationalisation process already under way," he said.
Ever smaller customers would be touched by competition.

"Competition for private clients may at its worst lead to that revenues from a customer flow abroad, but the core services the client needs, such as for instance cards, cashpoint machine networks etc., remain with domestic banks," he added.

Jannari said the state's quarantee to the banking system had been wise at the time when parliament approved it during the banking crisis but it had lifted moral hazard to international record levels. The state's unlimited guarantee of deposits had similar effects, he added.
"It's about time to remove these safety nets and return to business according to normal market economy," he said.
